utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we start with the next witness, there is just a little housekeeping issue that we'd like to deal with. Could we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls its next witness, MM-080, MM-080. We have to go into private session to bring him in? I'm sorry. Can we go into private to bring him into the room. I thought they could do it without broadcasting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the registrar every time he is on his feet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Registrar, every time you are on your feet please switch your microphone on. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us in November of 1991, who was the chief of the security department within the 9th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The chief of the security department in the 9th Corps was Colonel Tolimir Zdravko, Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 180th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the 180th Motorised Brigade was Colonel Stripko Cecovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The translation we got is Stripko, but is it that or Tripko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tripko, T.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us where Colonel Tripko Cecovic was based, where did he operate from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was based in the barracks in Benkovac. That was his command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What corps was the 180th Motorised Brigade in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the 9th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 9th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commander of the 9th Corps was Major-General Vukovic. His first name was Vladimir, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where was the command of the 9th Corps based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command of the 9th Corps was based in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions now about the Territorial Defence. In the autumn of 1991, who was the commander of the Territorial Defence in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the staff there was Zoran Lakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever see Zoran Lakic at the command of the 180th Motorised Brigade in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, his work-place was not in the command. He might come to see the commander for a meeting or talks or things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the police in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The chief of the police station was Bosko Drazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In November of 1991, was the JNA barracks in Benkovac blockaded, put under any kind of a blockade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did you mean the blockade by the Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the barracks attacked by Croat forces in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, we're now in open session, so I'll remind you to take care in your answers. Do you know why there was an attack on Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I wasn't present during the preparation or planning or whatever I may call it, the attack occurred because of frequent incidents or activities of the units on the Croat side. Some of their forces were located in Skabrnja, and they made incursions on the road between Benkovac and the Zemunik airport and the villages there. They opened fire on the JNA vehicles and the columns that moved along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you some questions about what you've told us so that we can be clear and precise, and to do that I'd ask that we see Exhibit 23 on the e-court. This is the atlas and specifically page 25 which has got ERN number, the last four digits 6421. And if we could -- yes, blow-up around -- yeah, and if we could blow it up even more. I'm interested in the part between Benkovac and Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the map there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you made reference to a road between Benkovac and Zemunik airport and you said: They opened fire on the JNA vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What I'm going to ask if you could take a pen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- and you're going to be given a special pen to do this. And can you take the pen and draw the road, mark the road, that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in November of 1991, is this the road that was being used by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In November of 1991, the road that went as far as Benkovci was used. What I drew here were the points where you turn towards the airport. But in November we used the road between Benkovac and Biljane Donje, then we had to take a turn towards Smilcici and take a round-about way to reach the airport of Zemunik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put a number 1 next to the road that was used during November 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the -- let me see if I'm clear on your testimony. Are you -- is it -- am I clear that in November of 1991, the road that was used was from Benkovac to Donje Biljane, up to Smilcic, and then left to Zemunik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I will mark that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you -- thank you. And if you could just put a number 1 up near Smilcic to indicate that road that was used in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarification. Does it mean that the route taken in November 1991 did not go along the road between Zemunik and Smilcic? Because it looks like it's now going in the field. There's a road there, very huge road, between Smilcic and Zemunik, but the pen that the witness used doesn't go along that road, it goes north of that road. Does it mean the JNA was travelling in the field to reach Zemunik from when they -- from the point in Smilcic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the road you mentioned, Your Honour, between Smilcici and Zemunik Gornji, that one was not used since it was blocked by the Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the road that you marked at the beginning of your answer, when we started using this map, that goes between Donje Biljane and Zemunik, was that road used during November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That road wasn't used either in 1991, but we went the way I marked it, from Donje Biljane up to Smilcic, where you see a circle marking a settlement, and then to the left through an orchard, which was a state-owned farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just so we're absolutely clear, could you just put a number 2 next to that part of the road that you marked between Donje Biljane and Zemunik that was not used in November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then -- it's -- could you draw a -- could you just draw a little line from that 2 to the road that it indicates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I put the number 2 next to the road between Smilcici and Zemunik Gornji.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I was not clear. What I wanted -- let's -- so that number 2 is for the road between Smilcic and Zemunik Gornji. Now could you put -- we'll use a number 3 to indicate --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- the road between Donje Biljane and Zemunik that was not used in November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of the roads were used. All of the roads going towards Zadar and the paths are marked going to Zemunik Gornji were not used at the time. The road Zemunik-Smilcic-Zemunik Gornji is the one. The other road between Skabrnja and Zemunik Gornji, I don't know if you can see that, that one wasn't used either. The only one we used was the one leaving Smilcic to the left, through the field. It is an unmarked path because such a map was never made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, can we understand what was the significance at the giving of making markings on this map of your drawing your line between Donje Biljane and Zemunik Gornji? What did you want to tell us about that line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I understood the Prosecutor's question, to mark the road -- the road that the JNA units were not able to use going to Zemunik Gornji. That's the first marking. And then I marked the one between Smilcici and Zemunik Gornji.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it is your testimony that the road between Donje Biljane and Zemunik Gornji was also not used by the JNA in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if I understood the Prosecutor's questions correctly, that is the road he wants you to mark with the number 3. Would you like to mark that with the number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if this now-marked map could be saved as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map, as marked by the witness, is admitted into evidence as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 784, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'm done with that map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when we started talking about the attack on Skabrnja and I asked you why -- you told us that you weren't present for the preparation but you gave some reasons that you thought. And you said that there had been -- you said: They made incursions on the road. And then you said: "They opened fire on the JNA vehicles." Is that what you meant by "incursions," that they fired on JNA vehicles travelling along that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also said that: "Some of their forces were located in Skabrnja." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the information we had, in Skabrnja there was an independent battalion of Skabrnja, as we used to call it, counting some 250 to 300 armed men. They also had mortars of 60- and 82-millimetre calibre as well as a part of their logistics was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are always pieces of information here and there gained through various channels. We got ahold of a newspaper that was published in Zadar, and their commander spoke about that in the paper. He was the man who commanded the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, we're now in open session, so again take care in how you answer my questions. You testified that you don't remember whether anyone had been injured or wounded. I just want to get some clarity on that answer. Are you saying that you have no memory either way or that you have no memory that anybody was injured or wounded? I'm not sure my question is clear, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Whiting is repeating the question that was already posed of the witness, and the witness provided a specific and precise answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the answer, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor previously had asked the witness whether he knew whether anyone was wounded in the shooting and the fire opened against the JNA vehicles, and the witness stated clearly that he can't remember. Therefore, I see no reason for pressing this further and to ask the witness the same thing yet again. Perhaps the Prosecutor expects the witness to state that he cannot remember whether there was any fire opened on the JNA vehicles after all, although we have received the answer to that effect already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, what are you saying, perhaps the Prosecutor ... I think the last part of your sentence is out of order, Mr. Milovancevic. But if -- I think the question that was being asked by the Prosecutor was to get clarity. Are you saying that you have no memory either way or that you have no memory that anybody was injured or wounded? And he wants to get clarity on the question that you say has been given, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the sense of the question, as you have just put it, I find acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you look at page 22 at line 15. That's exactly what the Prosecutor said: "I just want to get some clarity on that answer. Are you saying that you have no memory either way or that you have no memory that anybody was injured or wounded? I'm not sure my question is clear," and that's when you stood up. So if that is -- if you accept that question, then the question should be allowed as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, maybe I'll repeat the question because of the objection. Are you saying that you have no memory either way or that you have no memory that anybody was injured or wounded as a result of these shootings on that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's like this. I simply don't remember whether anybody was injured during that shooting or, rather, the action against the column and the JNA vehicles. Because -- well, I can't actually say whether I don't remember, have no recollection, I don't remember whether anybody was injured when the JNA was shot at from Skabrnja in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you say that -- in that last answer you say that the JNA was shot at from Skabrnja. Are you still talking about shootings that occurred on that road that you marked for us on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so when you say "from Skabrnja," do you mean from the direction of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean from the direction of Skabrnja, not directly from the place, the settlement, but rather from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understand. Did the -- these shootings that you've described, to your memory, if you remember, did they prevent the convoys, the JNA convoys, from travelling on that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to be clearer, more specific. The vehicles were moving from the direction of Benkovac to about Biljane Donje, and then they turned towards Smilcici, the road I indicated, and further on up. But they had to be more cautious so that the movement of the vehicles -- they slowed down. They had to move slowly and with -- exercise greater caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from what you have described, these shootings on the road from the direction of Skabrnja, were there any other attacks at the -- on the JNA at that time, in your area of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the area of responsibility of the -- towards the unit or from the direction of Skabrnja towards the road? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We got into this topic because you -- I asked you why you thought there was an attack on Skabrnja, and you've been -- you've described as one of the reasons you thought was because of these shootings on the road. Were there any other attacks on the JNA, aside from the shootings on the road, in the area of Benkovac in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I can't remember everything that happened and place it in November 1991, but as I say there was shooting from Skabrnja and from -- and this area was the -- under jeopardy most. No, I can't give a precise answer. I can't give you any precise information as to whether that did happen, whether there was shooting, when it happened. You know, it's been 15 years since that time, so I can't be quite prior in answering your question. Could you restate your question, please, ask it differently perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I will restate it. Aside from the -- what you have told us just now about there being an independent battalion located in Skabrnja and the shootings on the road that the JNA travelled on, are you -- can you think of any other reason as you sit here today that Skabrnja was attacked in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, specifically -- well, I just can't remember now. I can assume something, in view of the fact that I was an officer for a long time, but I don't think that would have any validity in respect of this case. Or, rather, it would be assumption on my part. Well, there you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've given us some specific facts that you think might have been the reason for the attack on Skabrnja, and you were quite clear that you were not involved on the planning on the attack. But you nonetheless have given some specific facts, that is the independent battalion in Skabrnja and the shootings on the road. So my question is: Did -- are you aware of any other specific facts that might have led to the attack on Skabrnja? And if you're not aware of them and if you can't think of any, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just can't remember. Nothing comes to mind what other reasons or what -- what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Let's -- let's turn now to the attack itself, which occurred the day after you learned that there was going to be an attack. Can you tell us who led the attack? Who was in charge of the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the operation was led by Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic, Momcilo Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was his function or position at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time he was the deputy commander of the brigade, deputy commander of the brigade or Chief of Staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 180th, the 180th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go now to the next day. What did you hear happened the next day? What's the first thing you heard or learned about what happened in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was in town on business and I heard from some people that lieutenant or Captain Stefanovic was killed, Miroslav Stefanovic, and some people told me that he was taken to the surgical clinic in town. I went there and when I arrived at the surgical clinic, I saw a nurse, met a nurse there that was trying to revive him but he was already dead. She was trying to resuscitate him. And next to him she showed me another soldier that had been killed or seriously wounded on that occasion, and that's how I learnt about it and that there had been fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say that you were in town on business, what town are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm speaking of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've asked specifically for Exhibit 107, and could we look at page 2 of the B/C/S, page 1 of the English. Can we zoom in on -- yeah, there we go. Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, can you see the name that is handwritten there on this page? It's page 2 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that name is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says Lieutenant-Colonel Momcilo Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that the person you told us earlier was in command of the operation in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at page 9 of the become and page 2 of the English. And if we could -- on the left there, there is a date 19/11/91. If we could zoom in on -- no, I'm sorry, you're absolutely right. That was -- but that's -- I'm looking at the one that's a little bit lower, the second version -- the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, just so the record is clear we're looking now on the page that has the ERN number 02006877 and we're looking midway down the page on the left?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And on the English, Your Honours, this appears on page 2 of the English translation on the bottom part of the -- the bottom third of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, could you read what is written there underneath the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It states: "The 19th of November, 1991" -- excuse me. "At 1700 hours to carry out the operation of cleansing or mopping-up of Zemunik, Skabrnja, Nadin from Ustashas." I believe it says Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what does it say after "Zemunik"? There appears to be a G there. What does that reference in your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that is the settlement of Zemunik Gornji.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And for the assistance of the Chamber, these three villages are visible on the atlas at page 25 in grid -- well, it's actually in -- overlaps two grids, D2 and C2. Now, if we could look, please, at page 10 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English. And on -- if we could -- on the B/C/S if we could in on the top few lines on the left, and the date entry there is 20/11/91.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, what page of the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's about a third of the way down the page on the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, can you read, please, what is written there at the top after the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm -- it -- and what I'm looking for is the sentence next to the date -- not below the date but next to the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "An analysis of the mopping-up action or activity M, S, Z, G in the 180th Motorised Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is the first letter -- what is the -- you read some initials. What are the initials, please, that you read? Can you read them again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you mane the blocked letters M, S, Z, G.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me approach it this way. What do you take -- what do you understand those letters to refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having in mind the area where we were, this should probably mean Nadin, Skabrnja, and Zemunik Gornji, the villages there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is that first letter an M or an N?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks like an M, but it could be an N, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In -- if you look at the context, what do you think it is, the context of this report and what you have just told us what you think it stands for, what do you think it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it is the letter N.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the name, the second name that appears on this page? Can you read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who that refers to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this is the Dragicevic who was the logistics commander at the barracks or for the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For which unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 180th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next name appears to be Djurica. Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was chief of artillery or a commander of an artillery unit, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Within what unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the 180th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now could we go to the right-hand side of the -- of this page in the B/C/S and there -- there's a -- underlined, if we could just focus on that. And this is -- we are now -- have to move to page 4 of the English translation. And for the record on the B/C/S we are still on 02006878, we're now on the right-hand of the page just below a line that goes across the whole right hand of the page. There's some three words written that are underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, can you read those three words, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try. "Analysis with the leadership," I believe. Those are the underlined words. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. If you could -- what's the first name that appear there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That says Bosko Drazic, although the S in the first name is a bit unclear. I believe it to be Bosko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is that the person you identified earlier as the chief of the police in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The second name that's listed there that's underlined, can you tell us what name that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zoran Lakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was that the person you identified earlier for us as the commander of the Territorial Defence in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now if we could turn, please, to the next page in the B/C/S and still stay on page 4 of the English. And I'd like to look at the left-hand top of this page and look at the second name that is underlined on this page. And just so the record is clear, we're now on 02006879.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And does that say "Lieutenant-Colonel Samardzic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was, I believe, the TO brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to the right side of this page in the B/C/S and go to the bottom part of the right-hand side of this page, the last name that's underlined there. And now we are on page 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There is a name there Tadic, do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was one of the commanders in the armoured battalion. Whether he was a platoon or a command -- company commander, I don't know, but he was one of the commanders of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was that armoured battalion in the same brigade or a different brigade if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they were from the second -- well, I can't recall. I think it was the battalion that was within the 221st Brigade or they may have been with the 180th Brigade, our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to the next page in the B/C/S, still on the same page in the English. And if we could go to the lower left of this page, and just for the record it's 02006830.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That last name there, Blagojevic, do you know who this person was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blagojevic was also one of the commanders, unit commanders, in the armoured battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And finally, on the right-hand side of this page, on the top, there is a name. And this is now on page 6 of the English. Jankovic, do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was also one of the commanders of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are all my questions about this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could now go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [The confidentiality of portions of the following Private Session has been lifted by order of the Chamber.]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I assume that you know that I am one of the co-counsel for the accused, Mr. Martic, and that I'm going to conduct your cross-examination. I must ask you something before I proceed, and that is to ask you to pause between my questions and your answers because, of course, we speak the same language but the interpreters need some time to interpret. So thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: (redacted) And now my question in that regard is this: What was the atmosphere and mood at the time? What was happening during that period in Croatia? I'm not only referring to Benkovac, but Croatia in general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, it was 1991 when people began to separate on ethnic grounds. Croats went to towns where the Croatian population was in the majority, for example, there was mutual lack of trust, distrust between people of different ethnic groups, specifically here between the Serbs and the Croats living there in that town. Then we saw the burgeoning, or rather, the Croatian Democratic Union took over control in certain strong points and leading positions and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So all that was taking place, was it, at the time when all that existed as a legal subject was the SFRY, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Croatia being one of its units. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted) did you know about the fact that the Croats were arming themselves in the area which was under your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you learn about that? When organised this arming and were armed units created in the Croatian villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, according to the information we received and that I had, the arming was along the party lines, the HDZ lines, as we referred to it in the local communes or in the villages, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mentioned the HDZ, and that is an abbreviation of the Croatian Democratic Community, right? The Croatian Democratic Union, the leading political party in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you (redacted) know what the programmes and goals of the HDZ was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the political programme of the HDZ party was principally to take-over power and authority in Croatia -- well, that was one of the main goals. And once you have taken over power and authority you know what all that implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did that imply? Was it secession that this implied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one of the programmes and goals of the HDZ was to create an independent Croatia, an independent state of Croatia, if you like to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear of a government decision of the SAO Krajina, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, dated the 15th of July, 1991, about the establishment and arming of the units of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac? Did you hear of a decision of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. Perhaps it was published under some different name or something like that, but no I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about November 1991, did the brigade of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac exist in that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who was the brigade subordinated to, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I can only guess or assume, but that wouldn't be what you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If there was any fighting going on, if any combat operations took place, was that brigade supposed to be under the command of the JNA and its officers, had there been any fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's a brigade. No -- well, actually I can't answer that question. It depends on a decision made by the superior command, who was subordinated or resubordinated to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're not sure, that's why you can't give me an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, I'm not sure so I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this is time for a break. It's 12.00 as far as I can see, and if you agree perhaps we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I agree entirely, Mr. Perovic. We shall take the break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when we discussed the reasons for the operation on the village of Skabrnja, you stated that you cannot remember any other incidents, apart from the ones in which JNA units were attacked from Skabrnja when they were moving towards Zemunik. Regarding that, I would kindly ask for --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would -- Your Honour, I would object. I think that misstates the testimony. I think the testimony was that the JNA units were shot at from the direction of Skabrnja, not from Skabrnja. Otherwise, if that's -- if that clarification is made I wouldn't -- have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I stated the very expression "from the direction of Skabrnja." If I was wrong, I accept the objection entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No, the record says you said "attacked from Skabrnja." So if you accept that, if you can just rephrase, from the direction of Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so right away, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the incidents and the shooting that came from the direction of Skabrnja on the JNA units which were moving to Zemunik. You also stated that apart from those incidents you cannot recall any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding that could we please have 65 ter document 2066 put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Once we have that on the screen I wanted to ask you whether you've ever seen this document. This is the document. Were you able to see it before and to familiarise yourself with the contents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This is a letter by the commander of the 9th Corps, General Vukovic, dated the 20th November 1991, sent to the naval district command and the command of the 5th Military District to the group in charge of communicating with the European Community Mission. Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the heading of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out paragraph 1 of the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean under number -- under the number 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can read it out loud, please, or if you'd have me read out that paragraph, if you prefer that, I can do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can read it out. "We regret to conclude that the members of the European Community Mission, instead of being neutral, have acted in a very biased way with regard to the Croatian party. Certain members of the mission make a lot of effort to carry out tasks of importance to the Croatian party as successfully as possible. Not one time, regardless of our persistent assisting have the members of the European Community Mission allowed representatives of our command and the VPO command to visit the barracks installations, and the families of the SFRJ armed forces, members of which have been under a total blockade for months. Almost nothing has been done to unblock the barracks and forward posts to secure their normal supply and communication with Sibenik and Split. They do not have basic human rights and minimum living conditions."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read out the first two sentences of the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We also concluded that the combat activities directed against our facilities have not stopped. We want to point out the latest incident when the fire was opened on the Rade Koncar barracks in Sibenik between the night of the 19th and the 20th of November, 1991. In the last four days the Zemunik airport has been under persistent attacks carried out by the Croatian party during which expensive pieces of technology have been damaged and men wounded. [Indisernible] activities and infiltration of sabotage terrorist groups were frequent." Those were the three sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This part that you've just read out, is that in keeping with what

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a way, yes. Generally speaking, the situation was such as this, the barracks in Sibenik and Split were indeed under a blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What about the barracks in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was blockaded, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the entire town of Zadar, are there as many as 11 barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact number. I remember some three or four barracks that I used to go to. I don't know the exact figure, but there were many military facilities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, on the 20th of November, 1991, being the date the letter was written, the Zadar barracks was blocked or put under siege.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall the date, but the barracks were under siege at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the decision from the Ministry of Defence and the General Staff on the attempt to deblock the barracks? That was the decision dated the 16th of November -- September, 1991. Have you heard of such a decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This part that you've read out tallies with what you knew about the events in the field at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, through the colleagues who worked in other barracks I learned about the siege and you could read it in the papers and see it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: To be precise, why was Zemunik of such importance to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the military airport including the air force academy used to train pilots.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your answers given during your testimony in chief, all the regular routes going to Zemunik were blocked or couldn't be used by the JNA; therefore, you used a dirt path through Smilcici and across fields. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The village of Skabrnja, Nadin, and some other villages are located close to the Zemunik airport. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document since it hasn't been up until now, this letter of the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry to interrupt. Just out of an abundance of caution I wonder if we could have a redaction at page 62 at line 3 and 4. I think it -- it identifies the position of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What identifies -- I beg your pardon. I'm looking at the wrong page. Line 1 -- 3 and 4. Okay. Mr. Perovic, you don't mind redacting that part it states on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accidentally used the words that the Prosecutor wanted to have redacted. That's why I wanted to remain in private session. It's difficult to remain focussed and to take care of every single word I utter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In any case, Witness, this will be redacted and remain unknown to the public?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for the record, may lines 3 and 4 on page 62 be expunged from the evidence, please, on the public record. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to suggest to move into private session because I believe there are going to be some questions which may compromise the measures undertaken with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [The confidentiality of portions of the following Private Session has been lifted by order of the Chamber.]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly - and please correct me if I'm mistaken - the aim of the attack on Skabrnja was to neutralise the independent Skabrnja Battalion, the Croatian battalion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I didn't take part in the planning of the operation and I didn't work together with those people, I couldn't know what their aim was. The aim is set out by the unit commander. He needs to define the final goal. Whether that is to neutralise or to do something else, well I can only speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: But what you do know, and you've stated so, that you knew of the existence of this independent battalion in Skabrnja consisting of some 250 up to 300 armed men. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the data was, and we could read it out in the paper as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: During the attack on Skabrnja or on any other occasion, were the JNA soldiers ordered to expel civilian population or to commit any crimes against civilian population? Do you know of any such order, be it oral or written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) were you able to observe that most of the JNA soldiers thought that they were fighting for some kind of greater Serbia? Could you see anything like that? I'm talking about the majority of JNA soldiers. Would you say they were fighting for a greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So the majority of soldiers did not hold this conviction, that they were fighting for some sort of Greater Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Now, along those lines, what about the officers, did the officers hold that conviction, that you would know of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And in that regard, one more question: Did they all consider that as soldiers and officers of the JNA on duty in Croatia, doing active duty in Croatia, that they were in fact in their own country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the conviction was that we were still in our own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that the operation on Skabrnja was led by Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic, that he was in command of that particular operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the law on total national defence, All People's Defence, was it established that joint operations, Territorial Defence and the JNA, that all units are subordinated to the Yugoslav People's Army. Was that what was stipulated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was like this, all this was regulated by the strategy of an armed struggle. Now, how a unit is subordinated to another unit and that kind of thing depends on the given situation from one moment to the next, from one event or operation to the next. But in principle, according to strategy, that is how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The first victim in Skabrnja that you learnt about was Captain Miroslav Stefanovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: He was a captain of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a JNA captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn of the circumstances he was killed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from what some people said, it appears that he got out of an APC, whether he wanted to help someone who was wounded or whether he wanted to take shelter, I really don't know, I can't remember. But at that point a bullet hit him, either in the back or in his chest. So those were the circumstances of his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that upon entering the village of Skabrnja, he left a tank and used a megaphone, a loud-speaker, to call upon the people not to shoot and to enable the JNA units to pass by, and that at that point he was hit by a sniper, and the soldier who ran up to him was also killed on that occasion. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that. What I heard was the way I described it to you, concerning his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have Exhibit 511 placed on the monitor now, please, and it is page 15 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you by any chance --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you by any chance know the page number in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour. It is 0400/5211. That is the page number, but I don't know about the English version. And it is page 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you the next document. Is that a list of the personnel in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says a list of the employees of the SUP in Knin from the 1st of February, 1992, to the 28th of February, 199 -- sorry, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Now, take a look at number 6, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Does it say "Goran Opacic" there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And does it say since when he was a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment. On the 20th of February, 1991, to the 31st of October, 1991, Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And on the 18th of November, 1991, was when the operation in Skabrnja took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So from this document it would appear that this man Opacic during the operation was not a member of the police. Would that be the correct conclusion to draw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly you also stated that you did not think you were trained or qualified to carry out investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to the extent needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You were shown Exhibit 107 here, being Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic's diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit Number 107 put on the screen, page 9 in the B/C/S. That is page number 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You were shown a part of the document by the Prosecutor, a part of page 2, its upper part. But on that page there is also another sentence concerning the 19th of November. There is an entry there. Could you please read it out. It is towards the bottom of the page on the left side. What was found after the operation in Skabrnja in terms of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you be more specific as to the part of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The left side, the bottom half underneath the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found it. "At 1700 hours," I believe it says "carried out the operation of mopping-up of Zemunik, Skabrnja, and Nadin from Ustasha was carried out. Gradina was taken over." And BD, I believe it to be an abbreviation for combat actions. In combat actions there were two killed. Whether this is "two conscripts" -- no, it says "two wounded, two plus one. One tank and one APC were damaged. Ustasha killed, one of which was a foreigner."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out what's in the brackets. Or is it illegible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Quite illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can make out it says "Kurd."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, now that you mention it. And eight Ustashas captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What about the weapons and materiel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says "seized" here. "82-millimetre mortars," it must be a mortar if it's 82 millimetres; "then one 60-millimetre mortar, one 120-millimetre mortar, 50 automatic rifles." Then -K, one recoilless gun, plus seven creates of 7.62-millimetre ammunition, plus 35 ROP" or "RDV," I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What does the RDV mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. If it says "ROV," that was the standard abbreviation for a hand-grenade or if it's RB it could be hand-held rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And all that weapon -- all those weapons were found in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that tally with what you knew of the events in Skabrnja as regards the amount of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this document previously, Bogunovic's diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You didn't even know he had a diary of such nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I perhaps clarify something? You said "diary."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I may have misspoken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a notebook that each officer is given to carry out his duties. He's supposed to note down the most important activities in his work during his workday, briefings with superiors, with subordinates. And then he enters such data in the official notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry to overlap with the witness, but, Mr. Perovic, there is something I would like to have clarified at this point. Looking at the translation of the exhibit in English, directly under the 19th of November, 1991, it reads as follows: "The operation of cleansing Zemunik, Skabrnja, and Nadin from Ustashas was finalised at 1700 hours." However, when the witness was reading himself, what it says in the B/C/S version what was referred to in the transcript is "mopping-up." Now, because of the different interpretation and the different meanings, I would like to get a clarification whether it is "cleansing of from Ustashas," or whether it was "mopping-up" or how the witness understands the term, please, before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I believe you understood the question -- or rather, the Judge's request to -- for clarification. When this cleansing or mopping-up or those settlements of Ustashas, what did the person whose notebook was mean, what sort of cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he meant to liberate a part of that territory, to cleanse it of the opposing side's soldiers. So he only had in mind soldiers, armed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And he termed them Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may ask -- if may ask -- I don't know, are you done? If I may ask another question. Again in this English translation, the weapons that are said to have been seized there are five 82-millimetre mortars; one 60-millimetre mortar; and one 120-millimetre mortar. The witness then went on to mention a few others which are not there on the English translation. I imagine, of course, that we would have to go by the original, but we don't have -- we were not able to read the original. Is that what -- is that -- does everybody confirm that what was said beyond 120-millimetre mortar is actually what is in the original text?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As far as I'm concerned, it is in the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I can confirm -- I can't confirm the translation, but I can confirm that the English translation is not complete, that there -- it only translates portions. And I believe in the portion Your Honour just indicated, those dots after 120-millimetre mortar indicates that it continues and not everything has been translated. So I have no reason to believe that it's inaccurate, but of course since I don't speak B/C/S I can't confirm otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is a handwritten document. Do you recognise Bogunovic's handwritten or do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please remove the document from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please, could we keep the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness could you please make sure that when you answer questions, you do so by saying whatever you want to say loud. If it's no, it's no. Don't shake your head, because if you shake your head, the shaking of the head doesn't get transcribed on to the record. Sorry, Mr. Perovic, Judge has ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just asking myself -- I should ask this question concerning this document now or after. It's then on the next page, but what we can clarify is the very first page of the original which is the cover of the whole pad. And this says "JNA," doesn't it? Could we show to the witness this very first page and enlarge the symbol so that we can see that and what is written under that. Something with "NA" and then [B/C/S spoken]. Yeah. Can you maybe explain this cover, as you said this is the official notebook of every commander of the JNA. Please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you please repeat the question. I'm not sure what I need to provide my answer against.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You were asked about this book being a diary or a notebook of another sort, and you explained something about the nature of this notebook. Can you repeat that and explain what is written on the front cover, as being shown on the screen now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we see on the screen is the cover page of the official notebook used by every and any non-commissioned and commissioned officer of the JNA. There we see the JNA coat of arms, which was standard issue for all official notebooks that we used to receive. Underneath it says "notebook," and I believe the first word is "official."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please continue. I will come back to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Now, back to this notebook, this official notebook, Exhibit 107. On page 10 in the B/C/S and on page 3 in the English version, there was this information contained consisting of four separate letters. Can we go on page 10 of the B/C/S, which is the original and then discuss the correct translation. The copy of these pages always contains two pages of this notebook. And of the copies it's page 10, it's one page after the one which we discussed before. And it's under the date of 20 of November on the top of the left side. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can. Can you read about this "analisa" and then the rest I can't read. We discussed the first of these letters, remember? In the English translation it's being explained as an M. We decided it could be an N also, so we may establish that once more. What did it say, "analisa"? And then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can decipher -- yes, can I go ahead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says "analysis" and here it says "actija," action of cleansing. Then the letters are M or N, then there's a S diacritic, Z, G in the 180th mtbr, which is short for motorised brigade, of course. Do you want me to continue reading?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: M or N and then in between are commas. Can you explain once more which commas this seems to be -- this seems to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. M, S diacritic, then Z, G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, that makes you interpret this whole acronym as meaning --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean how I interpreted the abbreviations, the letters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I interpreted them as Nadin, Skabrnja, and Zemunik Gornji.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just wanted to clarify because these commas only after the first and the second letter, which makes a difference in interpretation, compared to what is contained in the English translation. Thank you very much for this clarification. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
